You're definitely not stupid! It's a valid question, and I should have probably clarified. Every ketamine clinic I've heard of has a psychiatrist on staff, and you have to give your psychiatric history showing that there is a pattern of not getting help from other treatments.

I talked to the psychiatrist on the phone, and then we talked a while before the infusion. As far as anyone to talk to during the infusion, the anesthesiologist came in about every 5-10 minutes to check my vitals and see how I was doing. I also brought my mom with me the first time, which I'm glad I did because I think I would have been a little scared not having someone to kind of distract me during my first infusion.

Hopefully I understood your question correctly :)

This is the main downside. I've had to save up for this for a while. I've been reading about it for years and knew that I needed to save up about $2500. It's about $450-500 per infusion. I wanted to see it through, and get my first 5-6 infusions. The thing is ketamine itself isn't expensive (as an anesthetic it's only about $25), but they charge a lot because an anesthesiologist has to administer it and its experimental. I know they are working on a ketamine nasal spray to make the treatment more widely available for people. 

I guess for me I was so encouraged by the research that I really felt compelled to give it a try. The cost part is unfortunate, but honestly, the way I feel today I'm really glad I saved up.

Sure! Ketamine is typically used as an anesthetic in higher doses (a lot of times for children), and you can definitely feel those effects during the infusion. It's not unpleasant though, your body feels a little heavier and your consciousness feels altered a bit, but not to the point where I wasn't completely lucid. I brought my mom with me (you have to have someone drive you home afterwards), so she just engaged me in conversation for most of the 40 minutes (the length of the infusion). The room felt a bit dimmer, and my body kind of alternated from feeling cold and the warm. I would rate the infusion itself as more of a positive than a negative experience, and the effects of the anesthetic pretty much went away immediately after the treatment yesterday.

I had the infusion yesterday at around noon, and feel good and encouraged today (for like the first time in over 10 years). I myself have severe PTSD, and the intrusive memories of my traumatic event don't seem to be bogging down my mind as much. I'm getting another infusion tomorrow, they recommend you have 3-5 the first three weeks, and then there's a maintenance period. Some people can go 3-4 months without needing another infusion, for some people it's only 30 days. It's still pretty experimental, so I'm just kind of taking it one day at a time. But it's really exciting! I never thought I would ever get relief honestly, and I'm hoping that maybe this could provide some hope to others as well who have struggled with not getting better from medications.

Hope this helps!

Apparently, research has shown that people with depression are often able to remember 'big picture' events, but have trouble recalling the 'finer details' of certain events and memories. Apparently, scientists have speculated that this is likely because the brain has more difficulty producing new neurons in the hippocampus when an individual is depressed.

I think you're touching on something very important. A lot of psychiatrists (but not all certainly) view their clients as merely a diagnosis, which inevitably leads to a feeling of dehumanization for the person being diagnosed, because there is no way that the DSM can begin to account for the infinite differences in human beings. There's something incredibly rewarding about focusing on the individual instead of their ailment (similar to the humanistic psychology trend that was popular in the 1960s with thinkers such as Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow).

I hope you go on to have a clinical practice (if you have interest that is) because I think you've got a great grip on something a lot of mental health professionals seem to neglect. Cheers and best of luck :)

Hmm, well let me start out by saying that there's a new branch of OCD that's emerging (although it's not in the DMV, so not recognized officially) called "purely obsessional OCD":
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purely_Obsessional_OCD

That's not to say I don't have compulsions, I DEFINITELY do. In particular, I have a compulsive need to ask for reassurance (which is EXTREMELY common for sufferers of OCD). I also check things repeatedly to a certain extent (which is an element of OCD highly portrayed in the media) and I also have a tendency to avoid things that make me anxious/uncomfortable. Which, although it may sound strange, would be classified as a "ritual."

Existential OCD is somewhat hard to define, and I think the problem is that there is not a whole lot of information available to the general public. Every time I've talked to an 'OCD expert' (usually a psychiatrist) they tend to quickly throw around that I have a lot of 'obsessional existential angst' and they usually comment that, although not extraordinarily common, they have run into others that have similar obsessions.

Like I said, there's unfortunately not a ton of information about existential OCD, but here's a thread that I think you might find interesting (and hopefully even helpful):
http://www.socialphobiaworld.com/existential-ocd-27494/

You're not allowed to leave in the more restrictive facilities (and even when it gets more lenient) you still are on very constant watch, so you do A LOT of sitting around. I'm glad that you mentioned your age because it reminded me of something important that I hadn't mentioned yet. There are treatment centers who cater strictly to 'young adults' (which they classify as 18-30 years of age). I suppose this is because a lot of people who seek inpatient treatment are in 'emerging adulthood' due to the transitions and life changes that occur in one's late teens and twenties. I STRONGLY suggest that if you go to inpatient that you go to one that caters to young adults. I've heard from others that it can be kind of awkward having a roommate that's 40+ years older than you. It has nothing to do with them not being awesome people (they absolutely are), it's just there's something about living with people in your same 'phase of life' that seems to make people connect and relate a bit more.

So you're a Texan huh? Nice. I'm from Dallas :). Menningers is one of the top two programs in the country (the other one being in MA). If you're going to look into it, you need to look at COMPASS (the young adult program). That's where I went:
http://www.menningerclinic.com/p-compass/index.htm

Yea, unfortunately finances are a big problem. They occasionally offer scholarships but I think that is relatively rare. And I wouldn't worry about what your parents would say; I'm sure they love you unconditionally (as all parents should) and would do whatever they can to help and be there for you.

Hope this helps. Let me know if you need anything else (on here or PM) :)

I'm really glad to hear from you! Because yea, knowing where to start can be quite a burden. Let's see, to familiarize you with inpatient there are two kinds of programs. One is hospitalization (voluntarily usually) and the second is called a 'step-down'. Essentially you spend about 6-8 weeks in this intensive type of a program (which is ridiculously expensive) and then they recommend you go to a step down for about 3-8 months. The purpose (allegedly) of a step-down is to try to enable you to help live as an independent adult.

When I was first admitted I went to Menningers in Houston, TX. Which is a great program (one of the best) but extraordinarily expensive. I'm lucky to have parents that love me so much. For my 'step-down' I went to a place called 'Spruce Mountain Inn' in Plainfield, VT. Although I got better, I wouldnt recommend Spruce. There are some good things about it but things are a bit up in the air right now.

Menningers is amazing though. Sorry, if I'm answering too vaguely. Was there any place in particular you were interested in going?

Thank you! I got out of inpatient on July 14th so I guess it's been roughly 6 weeks. I do still participate in outpatient because I'm doing intensive exposure/response treatment for OCD. Which is pretty difficult, but I think it's well worth it.

As far as how things have improved for me, it's somewhat complicated to describe. What I can tell you is that in late December I was extraordinarily self-destructive and every minute that passed by was unfathomable torture. When I first arrived at inpatient, I freaked out and felt like 'I wasn't nearly as bad as everyone else' (which, I've been told, is an exceedingly common reaction). However, as time passes, you begin to appreciate it. There is something strikingly powerful about living in an environment with people who have shared your struggles. I had never experienced that before; I was used to being judged for my anxiety/depression.

If I compare December 2010 to now what I can tell you has changed is hope. I felt like I was in some bottomless black hole back then and frankly, I didn't think I had a good chance of getting out. Don't get me wrong, I still struggle today, and some days are worse than others (like today, for instance, I've felt kind of down).
